slots.text: Most founders validate ideas by asking "would you use this?" Wrong question. People lie about hypotheticals. Ask "how do you currently solve this problem?" then listen for pain in their current solution.

Three things that kill user interviews:

1. Leading questions ("Don't you hate when...")
2. Talking about your solution too early
3. Not asking for money/commitment at the end

If they won't pay for it, they don't actually want it.

Noticed a pattern: founders who build AI features first usually solve the wrong problem. The AI becomes the product instead of solving a real workflow issue. Better to find the friction first, then see if AI helps.

The hardest part of workflow automation isn't the tech—it's getting people to change their habits. You can remove 90% of the friction and still fail because humans resist new patterns, even better ones.
"Talk to users" is incomplete advice. Talk to users, yes. But also watch them work. What they say they do and what they actually do are often completely different things.

Signs your idea validation is actually just confirmation bias:

1. You only talk to people who already know you
2. You explain the problem before asking about it
3. You count interest as validation
4. You avoid talking to skeptics
Most founders skip validation because they think it means building surveys. It actually means selling before you build. Way different skill set.

User interviews that actually matter:

1. Ask about their current broken process
2. Get them to walk through it step by step
3. Find where they waste the most time
4. Ignore everything they say about features

The hardest part about building with AI isn't the tech. It's that users expect magic but can't articulate what magic looks like for their specific workflow. You end up building generic tools nobody pays for.
Founders who talk to 50 users before writing code ship faster than founders who talk to 5 users after building an MVP.
Friction isn't always bad. Sometimes friction is the only thing preventing your users from making expensive mistakes.

Signs your idea validation is working:

1. People interrupt you to ask pricing
2. They start describing their exact use case
3. They introduce you to their team
4. They ask when they can start using it

Most founders validate ideas by asking "would you buy this?" Wrong question. Ask "what did you do the last three times you had this problem?" You'll learn what actually happens vs what people think they'd do.

Signs you're talking to the wrong users:

1. They have lots of time to chat
2. They love giving product feedback
3. They ask when it'll be ready
4. They've never paid for a solution
5. They want features, not outcomes

Building with AI feels like having a really smart intern who hallucinates. Great at the first 80% of any task, completely unreliable for the last 20%. The trick is designing workflows where that 20% doesn't matter or is easily caught.
Every workflow has exactly one step that everyone hates doing. Remove that step and suddenly the whole process feels effortless. Add friction there and people abandon the entire thing.
User interviews are not about validating your idea. They're about understanding the problem space well enough that your eventual solution feels inevitable to users.

Three questions that actually matter in user research:

1. Walk me through the last time this was a problem
2. What did you try that didn't work?
3. What would have to be true for you to change how you do this?
Most founders skip validation because they think they know their users. But knowing someone exists and knowing what they'll pay for are completely different things.

Three things that kill user interviews:

1. Leading questions that confirm what you want to hear
2. Talking to people who are too polite to disagree
3. Asking about hypothetical future behavior instead of past actions

The hardest part about building with AI isn't the technical integration. It's figuring out which problems actually need AI versus which ones just need better UX. Most workflow friction comes from bad design, not lack of intelligence.
Founders who talk about "removing friction" usually mean adding more features. Founders who actually remove friction delete things.
User interviews should feel awkward. If everyone's nodding along and being supportive, you're not asking hard enough questions.

Signs your idea validation is working:

1. People interrupt you to ask pricing before you finish explaining
2. They start describing their current painful workarounds
3. They offer to pilot it immediately
4. They refer you to others with the same problem
Most founders think validation means asking "would you use this?" That's the worst question you can ask. People lie, especially when they're trying to be nice.

Three questions that actually reveal user behavior:
1. Walk me through the last time you dealt with this problem
2. What did you try that didn't work?
3. How much time/money did that waste cost you?
The founders who validate ideas fastest are the ones who already have distribution. They're not building audiences while building products—they built the audience first.
AI tools are making it easier to build solutions, but harder to find real problems. When you can prototype anything in a weekend, the temptation is to skip talking to humans entirely. Bad move.
Removing friction from your own workflow is usually a better business idea than removing friction from someone else's. You understand the pain viscerally.

Signs you're talking to the wrong users:
1. They have all the time in the world to chat
2. They love every feature you describe
3. They've never paid for tools in this space
4. They ask when it'll be free
Most founders validate ideas by asking 'would you use this?' Wrong question. Ask 'what's the most annoying part of how you handle this today?' Then shut up and listen.

Three things that kill user interviews:

1. Leading questions that get you the answer you want
2. Talking to people who are too polite to tell you the truth
3. Asking about hypotheticals instead of current behavior
Teams that build AI features first, then find use cases for them, ship stuff nobody actually needs. The ones that start with workflow friction and use AI to solve it build things people pay for.

Why do we overcomplicate idea validation? Because we're terrified of being wrong. So we add surveys, focus groups, competitor analysis. But the fastest way to be wrong is to avoid talking to real users doing real work.
The best workflow improvements are invisible. Users shouldn't think 'wow, this AI is amazing.' They should think 'weird, this used to take forever and now it doesn't.'
Founders who validate ideas by building full prototypes burn months on features nobody wants. The ones who validate with conversations and mockups kill bad ideas in days.
Most idea validation happens in spreadsheets and Slack threads. The actual conversation with users is maybe 10% of the work. The other 90% is synthesizing what they actually meant vs what they said.

Three things that kill user interviews:

1. Leading questions that confirm what you want to hear
2. Talking to people who are too polite to tell you the truth
3. Asking about hypothetical behavior instead of actual behavior

AI tools promise to automate everything but most workflows break because of human handoffs, not technical complexity. You can't prompt-engineer your way out of unclear requirements or misaligned expectations between team members.

Founders who validate ideas quickly tend to ask "what did you do last time this happened" instead of "would you use a tool that does X." Past behavior predicts future behavior. Hypotheticals predict nothing.
The hardest part about removing friction isn't identifying where it exists. It's convincing people that the 30-second workaround they've memorized is actually costing them hours every week.

Signs your workflow automation actually works:

1. People stop asking how to do the old manual process
2. New team members learn the automated way first
3. Nobody complains when the old system breaks
4. Usage goes up without any promotion
